title.value: Mitigating Goal Misgeneralization via Minimax Regret
title.justification: The title is clear from the beginning of the document and repeated multiple times throughout.
title.quote: Mitigating Goal Misgeneralization via Minimax Regret

analysis.description: This paper addresses the problem of goal misgeneralization in reinforcement learning, where a learned policy might pursue a proxy goal instead of the intended goal due to distribution shifts. It explores the use of minimax expected regret as an objective to mitigate such misgeneralization, both theoretically and empirically. The study finds that while commonly used maximum expected value objectives can lead to misgeneralization, minimax expected regret presents a more robust alternative.

type.justification: The paper is theoretical as it introduces new theoretical frameworks and proves results regarding goal misgeneralization and minimax expected regret.
type.quote: In this paper, we theoretically investigate the possibility of goal misgeneralization under maximum expected value (MEV) and minimax expected regret (MMER) objectives, and empirically validate our results.

name.justification: The paper discusses reinforcement learning, mentioning reinforcement learning terminology and problems such as goals, reward functions, and environment design.
name.quote: Safe generalization in reinforcement learning requires not only that a learned policy acts capably in new situations, but also that it uses its capabilities towards the pursuit of the designer’s intended goal.

name.justification: Goal misgeneralization is considered a specific type of failure in achieving AI Safety, focusing on ensuring that AI systems’ goals align with intended outcomes.
name.quote: A particular challenge arises when incomplete coverage of the environment space during training creates a proxy goal.

name.justification: The paper explores methods to design environments without supervision to better train agents against misgeneralization.
name.quote: For MMER, we use two methods of regret-based unsupervised environment design (UED; Dennis et al., 2020).

name.justification: Domain Randomization is used as a training method to examine its susceptibility to goal misgeneralization.
name.quote: Theorem 1 says that if the proportion of distinguishing levels in the fixed training distribution is small enough, then approximately optimizing MEV possibly leads to goal misgeneralization. Our experiments show that DR, an MEV-based training method, indeed exhibits goal misgeneralization when the proportion of distinguishing levels in the training distribution is small enough.

is_contributed.justification: Domain Randomization is discussed as a pre-existing method rather than a contribution of this paper.
is_contributed.quote: This is a nontrivial identity that does not hold for partially observable underspecified environments in which the level is not observable to the policy.

is_executed.justification: The paper conducts experiments to examine Domain Randomization's performance, suggesting it was executed.
is_executed.quote: Our experiments show that DR, an MEV-based training method, indeed exhibits goal misgeneralization when the proportion of distinguishing levels in the training distribution is small enough.

is_compared.justification: Domain Randomization is compared to other methods like MMER-based methods in terms of their effectiveness in handling goal misgeneralization.
is_compared.quote: We see generally that the more advanced UED methods are more robust to goal misgeneralization (Section 7.3). In KEYS AND CHESTS , MEV outperforms ACCEL with max-latest regret estimation, underscoring reliable regret estimation as a particular challenge for future work on MMER-based training (Section 7.4).

name.justification: Maximin Expected Value is analyzed in the context of its failure to induce robustness in reinforcement learning models.
name.quote: In this section, we discuss an alternative strategy to minimax expected regret for selecting robust policies. Namely, we consider the maximin expected value (MMEV) training objective.

is_contributed.justification: The model is analyzed theoretically, not introduced as a new proposition in this paper.
is_contributed.quote: Rather than modeling inductive bias, we characterize the possibility of goal misgeneralization.

is_executed.justification: The section discusses the theoretical aspects and drawbacks of MMEV, but does not detail any empirical execution.
is_executed.quote: This is because the agent has no incentive to improve performance in any level above the maximum performance in worst-case levels.

is_compared.justification: Theorems in the paper compare MMEV to MMER for their susceptibility to goal misgeneralization.
is_compared.quote: Dennis et al. (2020) argues that the MMEV objective fails to induce robustness in an environment where the optimal value of each level varies within the level space.

name.justification: JAX is mentioned as the framework within which several grid-world environments were implemented for the research.
name.quote: For each environment, we construct two procedural level generators Λ Ambig. , Λ Distg. ∈ ∆(Θ), approximately concentrated on ambiguous and distinguishing levels, respectively. From these, we define training distributions Λ Trainᵦ= (1 − α)Λ Ambig. + αΛ Distg. where α is the proportion of distinguishing levels. In our experiments, we vary α between 10 −5 to 10 −1 , with α ∈ {0, 1} as baselines. We evaluate on Λ Deploy= Λ Distg. , approximating a proxy-distinguishing distribution shift.
